strand.title: Geometry & measures
strand.metaDescription: GCSE geometry and measures: properties and constructions, mensuration and calculation, vectors.

topics.title: Properties and constructions
topics.cardDescription: Angle facts, polygons, congruence and similarity, constructions and loci, transformations, and circle theorems.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE properties and constructions: angle facts, polygon angles, congruence and similarity, constructions and loci, transformations and the circle theorems, with worked examples and the mistakes that lose marks.

subtopics.title: Points, lines and planes
subtopics.description: The vocabulary of geometry: points, line segments, vertices, edges, planes, polygons and what makes a polygon regular.
subtopics.coverNote: Define and use point, line, line segment, vertex, edge, plane, parallel, perpendicular, polygon and regular polygon, naming polygons up to decagon. Vocabulary and recognition only: angle facts start on the sibling angle pages, solids and their faces live on Faces, edges and vertices, and measuring belongs to Mensuration. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Labelling and drawing conventions
subtopics.description: Naming a side AB and an angle ABC, and the hatch, arrow and right-angle marks a diagram uses.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover side AB, angle ABC and the angle symbol, triangle ABC, hatch marks for equal sides, arrowheads for parallels, the right-angle square and equal-angle arcs, plus drawing a diagram from a written description, which G1 explicitly requires. Compass constructions are the Constructions group; actual measuring is Mensuration. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
subtopics.description: Lines that never meet and lines that cross at 90°, and the marks that claim each on a diagram.
subtopics.coverNote: Identify and mark parallel and perpendicular lines, use the arrow and right-angle conventions and notation like AB parallel to CD, and recognise both inside polygons and diagrams. Angle chasing on parallel lines belongs to the alternate, corresponding and co-interior pages; gradients of parallel and perpendicular graphs are Algebra's A9. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Naming angles by size
subtopics.description: Acute, right, obtuse and reflex angles named by size, and estimating before measuring so gross errors get caught.
subtopics.coverNote: Name acute, right, obtuse and reflex angles from their size ranges, order angles by size, and estimate before measuring so gross errors get caught. Protractor technique itself lives on Mensuration's Measuring lines and angles (G15); no angle arithmetic here, which starts at Angles at a point. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Angles at a point
subtopics.description: Angles meeting at a point sum to 360°, with reflex angles and several unknowns around one point.
subtopics.coverNote: Angles meeting at a full turn sum to 360 degrees, including reflex angles, several unknowns, equal-angle setups and simple algebraic angles such as 2x + 30. Require the written reason angles at a point. Straight-line and parallel-line facts are sibling pages; bearings applications sit on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Angles on a straight line
subtopics.description: Angles on one side of a straight line sum to 180°, and only when the line really is straight.
subtopics.coverNote: Angles on one side of a straight line sum to 180 degrees, with several unknowns, algebraic angles, and the check that the line really is straight before the rule is claimed. Reason stated every time. Co-interior angles, which also sum to 180, are their own page. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Vertically opposite angles
subtopics.description: Two crossing lines make two pairs of equal angles, and quoting the reason by its proper name.
subtopics.coverNote: Two intersecting straight lines give two pairs of equal vertically opposite angles: find angles and insist on the full reason vertically opposite angles are equal, not just opposite angles. No parallel lines yet — the transversal rules follow in the next group. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Alternate angles
subtopics.description: Equal angles in a Z shape between parallel lines, spotted from the diagram and quoted by name.
subtopics.coverNote: Equal angles in the Z configuration between parallel lines: identify pairs on marked diagrams, find angles, and quote alternate angles are equal. Distinguish from corresponding and co-interior pairs, which have sibling pages; chains mixing several rules belong on Multi-step angle problems. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Corresponding angles
subtopics.description: Equal angles in an F shape on parallel lines, and telling them apart from alternate pairs.
subtopics.coverNote: Equal angles in the F configuration on parallel lines, found on diagrams drawn in any orientation, with the reason corresponding angles are equal. Contrast directly with alternate pairs so the two names are not swapped; combined multi-rule chains go to Multi-step angle problems. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Co-interior angles
subtopics.description: Angles in a C shape between parallel lines sum to 180°, and why they are not equal.
subtopics.coverNote: Co-interior (allied) angles in the C configuration sum to 180 degrees: find angles, quote the reason, and stress they are supplementary, not equal — the standard error. The DfE names only alternate and corresponding, but every board examines co-interior at both tiers; derive it from those two rules. (G3)

subtopics.title: Multi-step angle problems
subtopics.description: Chaining several angle facts to reach the angle asked for, stating the reason for every step.
subtopics.coverNote: Chain point, straight-line, vertically-opposite, parallel-line, triangle and quadrilateral facts, stating a reason for every step, including algebraic setups and explain-why questions. This is where G6-style angle reasoning is rehearsed. Circle theorems are Higher pages in a later group; bearings journeys sit on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G3, G6)

subtopics.title: Types of triangle
subtopics.description: Equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles, and the side and angle marks that identify each.
subtopics.coverNote: Classify equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles by their side and angle marks, and combine classifications such as right-angled isosceles. State the angle consequences of each type, saving calculation for the angle-sum and isosceles pages. Congruence criteria are a later group. Both tiers. (G1, G4)

subtopics.title: The angle sum of a triangle
subtopics.description: Why the three angles sum to 180°, proved by drawing a parallel line through one vertex.
subtopics.coverNote: Derive the 180-degree angle sum with a parallel line through a vertex and alternate angles — G3 says derive, not just use — then apply it, including algebraic angles and triangles nested in other figures. The exterior-angle shortcut and the isosceles special case are sibling pages. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Base angles of an isosceles triangle
subtopics.description: The angles facing the equal sides are equal, and the two different answers when the given angle might be either.
subtopics.coverNote: Base angles opposite the equal sides are equal: find angles from a given apex or base angle, including the two-answer case where the given angle could sit in either position. The congruence proof of the fact lives on Proofs using congruent triangles. Both tiers. (G4, G6)

subtopics.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
subtopics.description: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it, in one step instead of two.
subtopics.coverNote: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: derive it from the angle sum and the straight line, use it as a one-step shortcut, and quote it as a named reason. Polygon exterior angles are a separate page. Both tiers. (G3, G6)

subtopics.title: Interior angles of a polygon
subtopics.description: Splitting an n-sided polygon into n − 2 triangles to find its angle sum, the quadrilateral’s 360° included.
subtopics.coverNote: Angle sum (n minus 2) times 180 derived by splitting into triangles, the quadrilateral's 360 included; find missing angles in irregular polygons and recover the number of sides from a given angle sum. Regular-polygon formulas and exterior angles each have their own sibling page. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Exterior angles of a polygon
subtopics.description: Why the exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360°, and finding a number of sides from one of them.
subtopics.coverNote: Exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360 degrees: justify it as one full turn, find a missing exterior angle, use interior plus exterior equals 180 on a straight line, and recover a regular polygon's number of sides from one exterior angle. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: Angles in regular polygons
subtopics.description: Each interior and exterior angle of a regular polygon, and which of the two to work out first.
subtopics.coverNote: Each exterior angle 360/n and interior angle 180 minus 360/n for regular polygons, taking the exterior route first; include regular polygons meeting at a point and combined-polygon diagrams. Deriving regular-polygon properties is exactly G3's brief. Irregular polygons stay on the interior-angles page. Both tiers. (G3)

subtopics.title: The special quadrilaterals
subtopics.description: The defining properties of the square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium and kite, set side by side.
subtopics.coverNote: Defining side, angle, parallel and symmetry properties of square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium and kite, stated precisely and compared, then applied to justify claims per G4's derive and apply. Diagonal properties and the inclusive hierarchy are sibling pages; area formulas live on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G4)

subtopics.title: Diagonals of the special quadrilaterals
subtopics.description: Which quadrilaterals have diagonals that are equal, perpendicular or bisect each other, and naming a shape from its diagonals.
subtopics.coverNote: Which special quadrilaterals have diagonals that are equal, perpendicular, bisect each other or bisect the angles, summarised side by side, and naming the quadrilateral that stated diagonal facts force. Proving diagonal properties with congruent triangles belongs to the congruence group. Both tiers. (G4)

subtopics.title: Classifying quadrilaterals
subtopics.description: Why a square is a rectangle but a rectangle need not be a square, and the most specific name the facts force.
subtopics.coverNote: Inclusive classification: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, every rhombus a parallelogram, with always-sometimes-never questions and the most specific name the facts force. Use the hierarchy to decide which properties transfer downwards. Builds on the definitions and diagonals sibling pages. Both tiers. (G4)

subtopics.title: Line symmetry
subtopics.description: Counting the mirror lines of polygons, and completing a shape so a given line becomes a mirror.
subtopics.coverNote: Count mirror lines of triangles, quadrilaterals, regular polygons and letter-style shapes, and complete a figure on a grid so a given line, including a diagonal, becomes a mirror. Symmetry as a defining shape property per G1. Reflection as a transformation producing an image is its own page. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Rotational symmetry
subtopics.description: The order of rotational symmetry as how many positions a tracing fits, and why order 1 means none.
subtopics.coverNote: Order of rotational symmetry as the number of fitting positions in a full turn, order 1 meaning no rotational symmetry; find orders for polygons and complete grid shapes to a stated order. Pair with line symmetry to pin down quadrilaterals. Rotation as a transformation is a later page. Both tiers. (G1)

subtopics.title: Congruent shapes
subtopics.description: Two shapes are congruent when one fits exactly on the other, mirror images allowed, corresponding parts matched up.
subtopics.coverNote: Congruent means identical in shape and size, mirror images included: decide congruence by matching corresponding sides and angles, including shapes on grids related by reflection, rotation or translation. The formal triangle criteria SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS follow on the next pages. Both tiers. (G7, G19)

subtopics.title: Congruence by SSS
subtopics.description: Three matched sides fix a triangle completely, so no angle needs checking at all.
subtopics.coverNote: Three matched sides guarantee congruence: check the correspondence, write it in matching vertex order, and explain why no angle information is needed. Marked diagrams and worded side lists both appear. Choosing between the four criteria is the Proving two triangles congruent page. Both tiers. (G5)

subtopics.title: Congruence by SAS
subtopics.description: Two sides and the angle between them, and why the angle must be the included one.
subtopics.coverNote: Two sides and the included angle: verify the angle sits between the matched sides, reject ASS as proof, and write the correspondence in order, including figures where a shared side supplies one matched pair. The right-angle exception RHS has its own page. Both tiers. (G5)

subtopics.title: Congruence by ASA
subtopics.description: Two angles and a matched side, and why AAS also works once the third angle is deduced.
subtopics.coverNote: Two angles and one matched side prove congruence, and AAS reduces to ASA once the third angle is found from the 180-degree sum; the matched side must correspond, not merely equal some side in length. Both tiers. (G5)

subtopics.title: Congruence by RHS
subtopics.description: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side, the one case where a non-included angle is enough.
subtopics.coverNote: Right angle, hypotenuse and one other side: the single case where a non-included angle suffices, and why — Pythagoras fixes the third side. Require the right angle to be marked or justified before RHS is quoted. Both tiers. (G5)

subtopics.title: Proving two triangles congruent
subtopics.description: Pairing up the given facts, choosing the criterion they satisfy, and why AAA and ASS prove nothing.
subtopics.coverNote: Assemble given and deduced facts — shared sides, vertically opposite angles, midpoints, parallel-line angles — choose SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS, and set the proof out with a reason per line and the criterion named. Show explicitly why AAA and ASS prove nothing. Both tiers. (G5, G6)

subtopics.title: Proofs using congruent triangles
subtopics.description: Proving results such as the isosceles base angles by finding a pair of congruent triangles inside the figure.
subtopics.coverNote: Use a congruent pair to prove results: isosceles base angles equal, diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, the perpendicular bisector construction works. This is G6's use known results to obtain simple proofs. Circle-theorem proofs stay on the Higher circle pages. Both tiers. (G6)

subtopics.title: Similar shapes
subtopics.description: Two shapes are similar when angles match and sides share one scale factor, so one enlarges onto the other.
subtopics.coverNote: Similar means equal corresponding angles and one ratio for all corresponding sides: decide similarity, including rectangles that are not similar, and connect similarity to enlargement. This strand owns the geometric reasoning; the scale-factor arithmetic is deliberately shared with the Ratio strand (R12). Both tiers. (G7, G19)

subtopics.title: Proving two triangles similar
subtopics.description: Two matched angles are enough to prove similarity, and why a shared angle alone proves nothing.
subtopics.coverNote: Two matched angles (AA) prove triangles similar: find the pairs in nested and bow-tie configurations using parallel-line angle facts, and show why one shared angle alone is insufficient. Formal statements with reasons expected. Length calculations move to the missing-lengths page. Both tiers. (G6, G19)

subtopics.title: Missing lengths in similar shapes
subtopics.description: Finding the scale factor from one matched pair of sides, then multiplying or dividing, never adding the difference.
subtopics.coverNote: Find the scale factor from one corresponding pair, then multiply or divide for missing sides — never add a common difference. Include nested triangles where the whole side, not the marked part, corresponds. Arithmetic duplicated with Ratio (R12) by design; area and volume factors are Higher siblings. Both tiers. (G19)

subtopics.title: A proof of Pythagoras’ theorem
subtopics.description: Why a² + b² = c², proved with the similar triangles an altitude cuts a right-angled triangle into.
subtopics.coverNote: A proof that a squared plus b squared equals c squared using the similar triangles the altitude to the hypotenuse creates, since G6 lists Pythagoras among derivable results. Keep it a reasoning page: numerical use, the converse test and 3D work all live on Mensuration's Pythagoras group. Both tiers. (G6)

subtopics.title: Areas of similar shapes
subtopics.description: A length scale factor k scales every area by k², so doubling a shape quadruples its area.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per G19's braces: length scale factor k gives area factor k squared, run forwards and in reverse via square roots, with mixed problems giving an area ratio and asking for lengths. Foundation stops at length factors on the sibling page. Arithmetic shared with Ratio (R12). (G19)

subtopics.title: Volumes of similar solids
subtopics.description: A length scale factor k scales volume by k³, and reading k back from a volume ratio needs a cube root.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only: a length factor k scales volume by k cubed, recovered by cube roots from volume ratios, plus mixed questions linking area and volume factors of one pair of solids. Requires the k-squared page first; density follow-ons belong to Ratio's compound measures. (G19)

subtopics.title: Constructing triangles
subtopics.description: Building a triangle with compasses from three given sides, or with a protractor from given angles, arcs left visible.
subtopics.coverNote: Accurate triangles from three sides with compasses, and from SAS or ASA with ruler and protractor, arcs and construction lines left visible; include impossible cases where the triangle inequality fails. Links the congruence criteria to drawing. Scale-drawing contexts sit on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G2, G15)

subtopics.title: The perpendicular bisector
subtopics.description: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of a segment with compasses, every point on it equidistant from the two ends.
subtopics.coverNote: Compass construction of the perpendicular bisector of a segment, equal-radius arcs from both ends, and the defining property that its points are equidistant from the two endpoints. Used later for loci and regions. Perpendiculars through a given point are the next two pages. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: A perpendicular from a point to a line
subtopics.description: Dropping a perpendicular from an external point with compasses, which is the shortest route to the line.
subtopics.coverNote: Construct the perpendicular from an external point to a line with compasses, and state G2's fact that this perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from the point to the line. Distinguish from the perpendicular at a point on the line, the sibling construction. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: A perpendicular at a point on a line
subtopics.description: Erecting a right angle at a marked point on a line, which is also the compass construction of 90°.
subtopics.coverNote: Erect a perpendicular at a marked point on a line by marking equal distances either side then bisecting — also the compass construction of a 90-degree angle, combined with bisection for 45. Arcs stay visible as evidence; protractor shortcuts score nothing in construction questions. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: The angle bisector
subtopics.description: Cutting an angle exactly in half with compasses, every point on the bisector equidistant from the two arms.
subtopics.coverNote: Compass construction of the angle bisector, with the property that its points are equidistant from the two arms; extend to constructing 60 degrees from an equilateral-triangle arc, then 30 and 45 by bisecting. Locus uses follow on Equidistant from two lines. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: Loci at a fixed distance
subtopics.description: The circle of points at a fixed distance from a point, and the rounded-ended band around a segment.
subtopics.coverNote: The locus a fixed distance from a point is a circle, and from a segment a stadium shape of two parallels and two semicircular ends; draw both accurately with compasses, including inside scale-drawing contexts. Regions inside or outside a boundary wait for Combining loci. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: Equidistant from two points
subtopics.description: Why the points equidistant from A and B form the perpendicular bisector of AB, constructed rather than guessed.
subtopics.coverNote: Points equidistant from A and B form the perpendicular bisector of AB: justify why, construct it, and shade the correct side for closer-to-A-than-B regions. Wholly construction-based — coordinate-geometry equations of perpendicular bisectors are A level, not GCSE. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: Equidistant from two lines
subtopics.description: Why the points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the angle bisector, plus the parallel-lines case.
subtopics.coverNote: Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the angle bisector, constructed with compasses and justified, plus the parallel-lines case giving the midline. Feeds straight into the region questions on Combining loci. Both tiers. (G2)

subtopics.title: Combining loci into regions
subtopics.description: Shading the region that satisfies several conditions at once, each boundary constructed and the correct side kept.
subtopics.coverNote: Regions satisfying several conditions at once: construct each boundary — bisectors, circles, parallels — shade the intersection, and keep the correct side of every boundary. Include scaled practical contexts such as goats, transmitters and treasure, with scale conversion leaning on Mensuration's scale pages. Both tiers. (G2, G15)

subtopics.title: Reflection
subtopics.description: Reflecting a shape in a mirror line on the grid, the diagonal lines y = x and y = −x included.
subtopics.coverNote: Reflect shapes in given mirror lines on and off axes: vertical and horizontal lines x = a and y = b, plus the diagonals y = x and y = minus x; images congruent, points on the mirror unmoved. Describing a given reflection fully belongs to Describing a transformation. Both tiers. (G7)

subtopics.title: Rotation
subtopics.description: Rotating a shape about a centre with tracing paper, where centre, angle and direction are all required.
subtopics.coverNote: Rotate shapes through 90, 180 and 270 degrees about a given centre — origin, vertex or external point — with direction stated and tracing paper allowed; images congruent. Finding the centre of a given rotation sits with Describing a transformation; rotational symmetry of one shape is an earlier page. Both tiers. (G7)

subtopics.title: Translation by a column vector
subtopics.description: Sliding a shape by a column vector, the top number moving it across and the bottom number up.
subtopics.coverNote: Translate shapes on axes by column vectors, top component across and bottom component up, negatives handled, and read off the vector between object and image — G24's translations as 2D vectors. Vector arithmetic beyond translation lives on the Vectors topic. Both tiers. (G7, G24)

subtopics.title: Enlargement from a centre
subtopics.description: Enlarging from a centre by a positive scale factor, with rays from the centre fixing where the image lands.
subtopics.coverNote: Enlarge from a given centre by positive whole-number scale factors, rays from the centre fixing image vertices, on and off coordinate axes; the image is similar, not congruent. Fractional factors are the both-tier sibling and negative factors the Higher sibling, so keep factors like 2 and 3 here. Both tiers. (G7)

subtopics.title: Describing a transformation
subtopics.description: Naming the single transformation mapping object to image, and the details a full description must state.
subtopics.coverNote: Give the single transformation mapping object to image with every detail: reflection needs the mirror-line equation, rotation the centre, angle and direction, translation the column vector, enlargement the centre and scale factor. Penalise combined or double answers; combining transformations is a Higher sibling. Both tiers. (G7)

subtopics.title: Enlargement by a fractional scale factor
subtopics.description: A scale factor between 0 and 1 shrinks the shape towards the centre, yet still counts as an enlargement.
subtopics.coverNote: Enlargement by scale factors between 0 and 1, shrinking towards the centre yet still called an enlargement, rays and centre method as before, describing as well as performing. Both tiers — G7's braces mark only negative factors as Higher, so those move to the sibling page. (G7)

subtopics.title: Enlargement by a negative scale factor
subtopics.description: A negative scale factor sends the image through the centre to the far side, inverted as well as scaled.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per G7's braces: a negative factor sends each ray through the centre to the far side, rotating the image 180 degrees as it scales, including factors like minus a half combining both effects. Describe as well as perform. Foundation stops at positive and fractional factors. (G7)

subtopics.title: Combining transformations
subtopics.description: Finding the single transformation equivalent to two done in turn, and the points a transformation leaves invariant.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G8): perform two transformations in succession, name the single equivalent transformation, and identify invariant points. G8's brief covers combinations of rotations, reflections and translations, so keep enlargement out of the combinations; describing single transformations is the both-tier sibling. (G8)

subtopics.title: Parts of a circle
subtopics.description: Centre, radius, diameter, chord, circumference, tangent, arc, sector and segment, the vocabulary circle questions are set in.
subtopics.coverNote: Label centre, radius, diameter, chord, circumference, tangent, arc, sector and segment on diagrams, and draw circles of a given radius — the G9 vocabulary the theorem and mensuration pages assume. No calculation here: circumference and area sit on Mensuration; the theorems are Higher siblings. Both tiers. (G9)

subtopics.title: The angle in a semicircle
subtopics.description: An angle subtended by a diameter is 90°, and spotting the diameter that triggers the theorem.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): the angle subtended by a diameter is 90 degrees; spot the diameter that triggers the theorem, combine with triangle angle sums, and quote the reason precisely. Often paired with tangent facts. The proof, via the angle at the centre, belongs to Proving the circle theorems. (G10)

subtopics.title: The angle at the centre
subtopics.description: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference on the same arc, however the figure is drawn.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, in standard, arrowhead and reflex configurations, with the semicircle case shown as a corollary. Full reason wording required; the proof lives on the proving page. (G10)

subtopics.title: Angles in the same segment
subtopics.description: Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, found by chasing the chord they share.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal; identify the shared chord, chase angles through multi-theorem figures, and quote the reason. Contrast with cyclic-quadrilateral opposite angles, the sibling result students most often conflate with this one. (G10)

subtopics.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
subtopics.description: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, and why all four vertices must touch the circle.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees, all four vertices on the circle; find angles including algebraic ones, reject figures with a vertex at the centre, and use the exterior angle equals the opposite interior corollary. (G10)

subtopics.title: Tangents to a circle
subtopics.description: A tangent meets its radius at 90°, and the two tangents from an external point are equal.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): a tangent meets the radius at 90 degrees at the point of contact, and the two tangents from an external point are equal, giving isosceles triangles and kite figures; combine with Pythagoras for lengths. The alternate segment theorem gets its own page. (G10)

subtopics.title: Chords and the centre
subtopics.description: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, tying circle problems back to isosceles triangles and Pythagoras.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, and radii create isosceles triangles, with Pythagoras finding half-chord lengths and distances from the centre. This is the workhorse fact for mixed circle problems and links back to Mensuration's Pythagoras pages. (G10)

subtopics.title: The alternate segment theorem
subtopics.description: The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, the theorem most often misquoted.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G10): the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment; identify which segment is alternate, apply it in multi-step figures, and quote the full name — the most misquoted reason. Requires the tangent facts page first. (G10)

subtopics.title: Proving the circle theorems
subtopics.description: Proving the standard theorems from radii making isosceles triangles, in an order that lets each proof use the last.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only — G10 says apply and prove. Prove the standard theorems with radii making isosceles triangles as the engine: angle at the centre first, then semicircle, same segment and cyclic quadrilateral as corollaries, plus the alternate segment theorem, and use them to prove related results. (G10)

subtopics.title: Shapes on coordinate axes
subtopics.description: Completing a named quadrilateral from given vertices, using its properties to fix the missing coordinates.
subtopics.coverNote: G11's geometrical problems on axes: complete a named quadrilateral from given vertices, find midpoints of sides and diagonals, and use shape properties to fix missing coordinates in all four quadrants. Equations of straight lines belong to Algebra; distances via Pythagoras sit on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G11)

subtopics.title: Faces, edges and vertices
subtopics.description: Naming the standard solids and counting their faces, edges and vertices, with prisms told apart from pyramids.
subtopics.coverNote: Count faces, edges and vertices of cubes, cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres — G12's full list — distinguishing flat faces from curved surfaces and prisms from pyramids. Euler's formula is enrichment, not required. Nets and elevations are sibling pages; volumes live on Mensuration. Both tiers. (G12)

subtopics.title: Nets of solids
subtopics.description: Deciding which flat arrangements fold into a given solid, and tracking which edges and corners meet.
subtopics.coverNote: Decide which flat arrangements fold into cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids, tracking which edges and corners meet, and sketch nets of given solids. Nets are KS2-KS3 carry-over — no G clause names them — but boards still set them, and Mensuration's surface-area pages lean on them. Both tiers. (G12, G13)

subtopics.title: Plans and elevations
subtopics.description: Drawing the plan, front and side elevations on squared paper, and rebuilding the solid the three views describe.
subtopics.coverNote: Draw the plan, front and side elevations of cuboid-built and simple curved solids on squared paper, and reconstruct or sketch the solid from its three views — G13 requires both directions. State which direction each elevation faces. Isometric drawing may support but is exam-board convention, not DfE. Both tiers. (G13)

groups.title: Lines, angles and labelling
groups.lead: The words, marks and conventions a diagram is written in, and the angle facts that hold at points and on lines.

groups.title: Angles on parallel lines
groups.lead: The three angle pairs a transversal makes with parallel lines, and multi-step problems that chain them together with reasons.

groups.title: Angles in triangles and polygons
groups.lead: The angle sum a triangle forces on every polygon, and the extra structure isosceles triangles and regular polygons carry.

groups.title: Quadrilaterals and symmetry
groups.lead: What defines each special quadrilateral, the diagonal properties that tell them apart, and the two symmetries a flat shape can carry.

groups.title: Congruent triangles
groups.lead: The four criteria that force two triangles to be identical, and the proofs congruent triangles unlock.

groups.title: Similar shapes
groups.lead: When two shapes count as similar, the reasoning that proves it, and how one scale factor controls lengths, areas and volumes.

groups.title: Constructions and loci
groups.lead: The ruler-and-compass constructions, the loci each one draws, and the regions that satisfy several conditions at once.

groups.title: Transformations
groups.lead: The four transformations on axes, described precisely, extended at Higher tier to fractional and negative enlargement.

groups.title: Circles and their theorems
groups.lead: The names for a circle’s parts, then the Higher-tier theorems that control its angles, applied with reasons and proved.

groups.title: Solids, plans and coordinates
groups.lead: Flat representations of solid shapes — counts of faces and edges, nets, plans and elevations — and shape problems pinned to coordinate axes.

topics.title: Mensuration and calculation
topics.cardDescription: Scale drawings and bearings, area, circles, volume, Pythagoras’ theorem, trigonometry, and the sine and cosine rules.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE mensuration and calculation: perimeter, area and volume, circles and sectors, bearings, Pythagoras’ theorem, trigonometry, and the sine and cosine rules.

subtopics.title: Measuring lines and angles
subtopics.description: Measuring segments to the nearest millimetre and angles with a protractor, using the scale that starts at zero.
subtopics.coverNote: Measure and draw segments to the nearest millimetre and angles to the nearest degree, choosing the protractor scale that starts from zero, with reflex angles by subtraction from 360. Estimate first to catch gross errors. Compass constructions live on Properties; bearings follow later in this topic. Both tiers. (G15)

subtopics.title: Units in perimeter, area and volume
subtopics.description: Why areas carry square units and volumes cubic units, and converting every length to one unit before calculating.
subtopics.coverNote: Why perimeter carries length units, area square units and volume cubic units, and converting every length to a single unit before any formula is applied. Boundary: unit conversion itself — including square and cubic unit conversion and compound measures — is taught on the Number strand's Measures and accuracy topic. Both tiers. (G14)

subtopics.title: Scale drawings
subtopics.description: Reading and making drawings at a stated scale, converting between drawn length and real length in both directions.
subtopics.coverNote: Interpret and produce drawings at stated scales like 1 cm to 5 km, converting drawn to real lengths and back, and measure accurately from the drawing as part of the answer. Ratio scales such as 1 to 25000 are the Map scales page; bearings combine on later pages. Both tiers. (G15, R2)

subtopics.title: Map scales
subtopics.description: Ratio scales such as 1:25 000 turned into real distances and back, with the unit change saved for last.
subtopics.coverNote: Unitless ratio scales such as 1 to 25000: convert map to ground and back, doing the unit change last, and choose sensible units for the answer. Shared territory with Ratio's scale work (R2); this page owns the map reading. Worded scales sit on Scale drawings. Both tiers. (G15, R2)

subtopics.title: Three-figure bearings
subtopics.description: Directions measured clockwise from north and always written with three figures, so 45° is recorded as 045°.
subtopics.coverNote: Bearings measured clockwise from north and always written with three figures, 045 not 45: read, measure, draw and state the bearing of one point from another, including on scale drawings. Back bearings and journey calculations are the sibling page; trigonometry on bearings diagrams waits for the trig pages. Both tiers. (G15)

subtopics.title: Calculating with bearings
subtopics.description: The bearing back the other way, and journey diagrams solved with parallel north lines and angle facts.
subtopics.coverNote: The return bearing by adding or subtracting 180, and bearings at the second leg of a journey found with parallel north lines and alternate or co-interior angles. Whole-degree angle reasoning only: Pythagoras and trigonometry on bearings diagrams belong to those pages, the sine and cosine rules being Higher. Both tiers. (G15, G3)

subtopics.title: Perimeter
subtopics.description: The distance round a shape, including deducing the unmarked sides of a rectilinear shape before adding.
subtopics.coverNote: Perimeter of rectilinear and straight-sided shapes, deducing the unmarked sides of L-shapes before adding, with simple algebraic perimeters included. Circles enter at Circumference of a circle, and shapes with curved edges at Semicircles and quarter circles; keep perimeter distinct from area throughout. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Area of a rectangle
subtopics.description: Area as the squares a shape covers, counted first and then found faster as length times width.
subtopics.coverNote: Area as squares covered, counted on grids then computed as length times width, the square as special case, and a missing side recovered from a given area. Rectangle area is KS2 carry-over that the G16 formula list assumes. Compound rectilinear shapes wait for the composite page. Both tiers. (G16, G17)

subtopics.title: Area of a triangle
subtopics.description: Half of base times height, where the height is perpendicular to the base and never the slant side.
subtopics.coverNote: Half base times height with the perpendicular height, never the slant side, in any orientation including obtuse triangles where the height falls outside. G16 lists this formula among those to know and apply. The Higher alternative half ab sin C has its own page in the sine-and-cosine-rules group. Both tiers. (G16)

subtopics.title: Area of a parallelogram
subtopics.description: Base times perpendicular height, and why using the slant side gives an answer that is always too big.
subtopics.coverNote: Base times perpendicular height, with diagrams deliberately labelling the slant side as a distractor; explain by shearing or cutting to a rectangle why the slant answer is always too big. G16 lists the formula among those to know. The rhombus uses the same formula. Both tiers. (G16)

subtopics.title: Area of a trapezium
subtopics.description: Half the sum of the parallel sides times the height between them, and identifying which sides are parallel.
subtopics.coverNote: Half the sum of the parallel sides times the height between them, the parallel sides identified first, derived by doubling into a parallelogram. G16 lists the trapezium formula among those to know and apply. Reverse problems continue on Finding a length from an area. Both tiers. (G16)

subtopics.title: Finding a length from an area
subtopics.description: Running an area formula backwards to recover a base, height or parallel side from the stated area.
subtopics.coverNote: Run the rectangle, triangle, parallelogram and trapezium formulas backwards to recover a base, height or parallel side from a stated area, substituting then solving a one- or two-step equation. Circle and sector reversals live on their own pages in the circles group. Both tiers. (G16, G17)

subtopics.title: Perimeter and area of composite shapes
subtopics.description: Splitting a compound shape into rectangles and triangles, or subtracting a hole, keeping perimeter and area separate.
subtopics.coverNote: Split compound rectilinear and triangle-based shapes into known pieces, or subtract a cut-out, deducing missing sides first; keep perimeter and area clearly separate when both are asked. Shapes involving circle parts belong to Semicircles and quarter circles; composite solids come later. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Circumference of a circle
subtopics.description: C = πd or 2πr, and deciding whether the given length is a radius or a diameter first.
subtopics.coverNote: C equals pi d or 2 pi r — G17 names these among formulae to know — deciding first whether the given length is a radius or a diameter, rounding sensibly, and reversing to find d or r from a given circumference. Exact-pi answers and part circles are sibling pages. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Area of a circle
subtopics.description: A = πr² with only the radius squared, halving a given diameter before anything is substituted.
subtopics.coverNote: A equals pi r squared, a formula G17 says must be known, squaring only the radius and halving any given diameter before substituting; reverse from area to radius with a square root. Contrast with circumference so the two formulas are not swapped. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Answers in terms of π
subtopics.description: Leaving circle answers as exact multiples of π instead of decimals, and calculating with them unrounded.
subtopics.coverNote: Leave circle answers as exact multiples of pi, add and subtract such multiples unrounded, and give exact or rounded answers as the question demands. Exact calculation with multiples of pi is the Number strand's N8; here it meets circles, arcs, sectors and cylinder volumes. Both tiers. (G17, N8)

subtopics.title: Semicircles and quarter circles
subtopics.description: Halving or quartering the circle formulas, and adding the straight edges whenever a perimeter is wanted.
subtopics.coverNote: Areas and perimeters of semicircles and quarter circles: halve or quarter the circle formulas, then add the diameter or two radii whenever a perimeter is asked — the classic omission. Compound shapes with circular parts included. General sector angles move to Arc length and Area of a sector. Both tiers. (G17, G18)

subtopics.title: Arc length
subtopics.description: The angle over 360 as the fraction of the circumference an arc takes, plus two radii for a sector’s perimeter.
subtopics.coverNote: Arc length as the angle over 360 of the circumference, plus two radii for a sector's perimeter, exact and rounded, major arcs via the reflex angle. G18 makes arcs and sectors both tiers, not Higher. Reversed problems recovering the angle sit on Finding the angle of a sector. (G18)

subtopics.title: Area of a sector
subtopics.description: The angle over 360 applied to πr² for the area a sector sweeps, and to nothing else.
subtopics.coverNote: Sector area as the angle over 360 applied to pi r squared and to nothing else — not to the circumference formula — with exact-pi and rounded answers, minor and major sectors. Both tiers under G18. Segment areas need the Higher formula half ab sin C, so they stay off Foundation. (G18)

subtopics.title: Finding the angle of a sector
subtopics.description: Running the arc and sector formulas backwards to recover the angle or radius from a stated length or area.
subtopics.coverNote: Rearrange the arc and sector formulas to recover the angle from a stated arc length or area, or the radius, as G18's angles explicitly allows, checking answers against 360. Requires confident rearrangement; the forward calculations are the two sibling pages. Both tiers. (G18)

subtopics.title: Volume of a cuboid
subtopics.description: Length times width times height counted as layers of unit cubes, and a missing edge from a stated volume.
subtopics.coverNote: Length times width times height understood as layers of unit cubes, the cube as special case, and a missing edge recovered from a stated volume. G16 lists the cuboid formula among those to know. Capacity conversions such as litres belong to the Number strand's measures pages. Both tiers. (G16)

subtopics.title: Volume of a prism
subtopics.description: Cross-section area times length for any prism, once the face that repeats has been correctly identified.
subtopics.coverNote: Cross-section area times length for any right prism — a G16 formula to know — identifying the repeating face first, with triangular, trapezoidal and L-shaped cross-sections. Cylinders follow as the circular case; oblique solids are beyond GCSE and the frustum is the Higher page. Both tiers. (G16)

subtopics.title: Volume of a cylinder
subtopics.description: πr²h as a circular prism, left in terms of π unless a decimal is demanded.
subtopics.coverNote: Pi r squared h as the prism with circular cross-section, exact in terms of pi or rounded, the radius halved from a given diameter first, and reverse problems finding h or r. Hollow cylinders and combined solids belong to Composite solids. Both tiers. (G16, G17)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a cuboid
subtopics.description: Adding the areas of the three pairs of matching faces, in square units although the shape is solid.
subtopics.coverNote: Total surface area as three pairs of congruent rectangular faces, computed systematically and given in square units despite the solid context, with painted-face and wrapping applications. Nets, taught on Properties, justify the count. General prisms are the next page. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a prism
subtopics.description: Adding every face of the net so none is missed, the two matching cross-section faces included.
subtopics.coverNote: Surface area of triangular and other right prisms by listing every face from the net — two cross-sections plus one rectangle per edge — so none is missed or double-counted. Slant faces may need Pythagoras first. Cylinders have their own page; painted composite solids come later. Both tiers. (G17, G20)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a cylinder
subtopics.description: The curved face unrolled into a rectangle 2πr long, plus two circular ends when the cylinder is closed.
subtopics.coverNote: The curved surface unrolled to a rectangle 2 pi r by h, plus two circular ends only when the cylinder is closed; distinguish open pipes and labels from closed tins, exact or rounded. G17 requires calculating this, while the circle formulas inside it must be known. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Volume of a pyramid
subtopics.description: One third of the base area times the perpendicular height, whatever polygon forms the base.
subtopics.coverNote: One third of base area times perpendicular height for pyramids on any polygonal base, distinguishing perpendicular height from slant edge. G17 requires calculating with this formula and does not list it among those to know by heart. Cones are the circular sibling; frustums are Higher. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Volume of a cone
subtopics.description: ⅓πr²h with the perpendicular height rather than the slant, and Pythagoras to convert between the two.
subtopics.coverNote: One third of pi r squared h with the perpendicular height, using Pythagoras to move between height, radius and slant height when needed, exact-pi and rounded answers. G17 asks for calculation, not recall, of the formula. The frustum, a Higher page, subtracts a similar cone. Both tiers. (G17, G20)

subtopics.title: Volume of a sphere
subtopics.description: Four thirds of πr³ with only the radius cubed, and hemispheres taken as exact halves.
subtopics.coverNote: Four thirds of pi r cubed, cubing only the radius, hemispheres as exact halves, and reverse problems recovering r by cube root. G17 requires calculating with the formula, which it does not list among those to know. Composite solids with hemispheres follow. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a pyramid
subtopics.description: The base plus the triangular faces, each triangle needing its own slant height rather than the solid’s.
subtopics.coverNote: The base plus congruent triangular faces, each triangle using its own face slant height, found by Pythagoras from half the base and the perpendicular height — not the solid's edge length. Square-based pyramids dominate. G17 requires calculation, not memorised formulas, here. Both tiers. (G17, G20)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a cone
subtopics.description: The curved surface πrl with l the slant height, adding the base circle only when the cone is closed.
subtopics.coverNote: Curved surface pi r l with l the slant height, adding the base circle only when the cone is closed, and Pythagoras converting between perpendicular and slant heights. G17 requires calculating, not memorising, pi r l. Frustum surfaces are rarely set and stay off this page. Both tiers. (G17, G20)

subtopics.title: Surface area of a sphere
subtopics.description: 4πr² for the whole sphere, and why a hemisphere’s total is 3πr² once the flat face joins in.
subtopics.coverNote: Four pi r squared for the sphere and 3 pi r squared for a solid hemisphere once the flat disc joins, exact and rounded, with reverse problems recovering the radius. G17 requires calculation with the formula rather than recall. Composite solids pairing hemispheres with cylinders or cones come next. Both tiers. (G17)

subtopics.title: Composite solids
subtopics.description: Volumes and surface areas of solids built from simpler ones, subtracting the faces hidden where the parts meet.
subtopics.coverNote: Volumes and surface areas of solids built from cuboids, prisms, cylinders, cones, hemispheres and pyramids: volumes add, but surface areas must subtract the hidden faces where parts meet. G17 names composite solids at both tiers. The frustum, conventionally Higher, has its own page. (G17)

subtopics.title: Volume of a frustum
subtopics.description: A cone with its top removed, its volume the large cone’s minus the similar small cone’s.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher by convention: frustum volume as the large cone minus the similar small cone, the missing cone's dimensions found by similar-triangle ratios, answers exact or rounded. The DfE never names frustums — they sit under G17's composite solids with G19 similarity — hence the similarity prerequisite. (G17, G19)

subtopics.title: Pythagoras’ theorem
subtopics.description: The squares on the two shorter sides sum to the square on the hypotenuse, which always faces the right angle.
subtopics.coverNote: a squared plus b squared equals c squared with c always opposite the right angle — G20 lists the formula among those to know — finding hypotenuses in 2D, answers as surds or rounded decimals, units consistent first. Shorter sides, coordinate distances, the converse and 3D each have sibling pages. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: Finding a shorter side
subtopics.description: Subtracting squares instead of adding when the hypotenuse is already known, the swap most wrong answers miss.
subtopics.coverNote: Rearranged Pythagoras: subtract squares when the hypotenuse is already known — the error-prone swap, named and drilled — with isosceles-triangle heights and ladder contexts. Purely right-angled 2D work; the cosine rule generalisation is Higher, in the sine-and-cosine-rules group. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: The distance between two points
subtopics.description: The straight-line distance between two coordinates as the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle the grid supplies.
subtopics.coverNote: The distance between coordinate points as the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle the grid supplies, coordinate differences as the two legs, surd or rounded answers, no memorised distance formula required. Links G11's coordinate problems with G20. Midpoints stay on Properties' coordinate page. Both tiers. (G20, G11)

subtopics.title: Testing for a right angle
subtopics.description: The converse of Pythagoras: checking whether the three sides satisfy a² + b² = c² before claiming the right angle.
subtopics.coverNote: The converse of Pythagoras: test whether a squared plus b squared equals c squared for the three given sides, c the longest, before claiming or denying a right angle, with Pythagorean triples and scaled triples featured. State the conclusion alongside the test. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: Pythagoras in three dimensions
subtopics.description: The diagonal of a cuboid found by two right-angled triangles in turn, one lying flat and one standing.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only — G20 braces three-dimensional figures. Space diagonals of cuboids via two chained right-angled triangles, heights of pyramids and cones, and face diagonals distinguished from space diagonals. Foundation Pythagoras stays in two dimensions on the earlier pages of this group. (G20)

subtopics.title: The trigonometric ratios
subtopics.description: Sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of sides, labelled hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent from the angle in use.
subtopics.coverNote: Define sin, cos and tan as side ratios — formulas G20 says must be known — labelling hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent relative to the chosen angle, in any orientation. Right-angled triangles only: general triangles are Higher, in the sine and cosine rules group. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: Finding a side with trigonometry
subtopics.description: Choosing the ratio that links the known angle to the wanted side, and when to multiply or divide.
subtopics.coverNote: Choose the ratio linking the known angle and given side to the wanted side, multiplying when the unknown is the numerator and dividing when it is the denominator, calculator in degrees mode. Right-angled triangles only, diagrams in all orientations; angles come next. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: Finding an angle with trigonometry
subtopics.description: The inverse functions sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ turning a ratio of two sides back into the angle.
subtopics.coverNote: Recover an angle from two known sides with inverse sin, cos and tan, choosing the correct side pair first, answers typically to one decimal place; read the inverse notation as the angle whose sine is, never as a reciprocal. Right-angled triangles only. Both tiers. (G20)

subtopics.title: Exact trigonometric values
subtopics.description: The exact values of sin and cos at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and tan up to 60°, read from two special triangles.
subtopics.coverNote: G21's exact values, both tiers: sin and cos at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, and tan at 0, 30, 45 and 60 only — tan 90 is undefined and outside G21. Derive from the half-equilateral and right-isosceles triangles for non-calculator questions. Surd arithmetic support is Number's N8. (G21)

subtopics.title: Angles of elevation and depression
subtopics.description: Looking up and looking down turned into right-angled triangles, the depression angle placed inside by alternate angles.
subtopics.coverNote: Elevation looking up and depression looking down, both measured from the horizontal: turn worded and pictured contexts into right-angled triangles, using alternate angles to bring a depression angle inside the triangle. Applications of G20 trigonometry, bearings mixes included; non-right-angled versions are Higher. Both tiers. (G20, G15)

subtopics.title: Trigonometry in three dimensions
subtopics.description: The angle between a line and a plane, found by building the right-angled triangle that contains it.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per G20's braces: the angle between a line and a plane, located by dropping a perpendicular and building the right-angled triangle that contains it, in cuboids, wedges and pyramids, usually after 3D Pythagoras. The angle between two planes is A level, not GCSE. (G20)

subtopics.title: The sine rule for sides
subtopics.description: Each side over the sine of its opposite angle is constant, so one matched pair unlocks the rest.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only — G22 names the sine rule among formulas to know and apply. Find a side from a matched angle-opposite pair plus one more angle, finding third angles via 180 first when needed. Choosing between the rules has its own page; the obtuse ambiguity sits on the angles page. (G22)

subtopics.title: The sine rule for angles
subtopics.description: The rule flipped to find an angle, and the second obtuse solution the sine of an angle can hide.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only: the sine rule inverted to find angles, including the ambiguous case where the sine gives both an acute and an obtuse candidate and the diagram or context selects one. G22 requires knowing and applying the rule; sides are the sibling page. (G22)

subtopics.title: The cosine rule for sides
subtopics.description: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C for the side facing a known included angle, with the subtraction done last.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G22, formula to know): c squared equals a squared plus b squared minus 2ab cos C for the third side from two sides and the included angle, evaluating the subtraction last and square-rooting at the end; an obtuse included angle makes the cosine negative. (G22)

subtopics.title: The cosine rule for angles
subtopics.description: The cosine rule rearranged to find any angle from three sides, a negative cosine signalling an obtuse angle.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only: the cosine rule rearranged to find any angle from three sides, a negative cosine correctly yielding an obtuse angle, with the largest-angle-faces-longest-side check. G22 requires knowing and applying the rule; no right angle may be assumed anywhere in the triangle. (G22)

subtopics.title: The area formula ½ab sin C
subtopics.description: Half the product of two sides and the sine of the included angle, no perpendicular height required.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (G23): area equals half ab sin C with the included angle, no perpendicular height required, run forwards for areas and backwards for a side or angle — G23 explicitly includes all three. Feeds segment-area problems alongside sectors; exact trig values give non-calculator variants. (G23, G21)

subtopics.title: Choosing between the rules
subtopics.description: Deciding from the given sides and angles whether right-angled trigonometry, the sine rule or the cosine rule applies.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only: the decision procedure — a right angle means SOHCAHTOA or Pythagoras, an angle-opposite pair means sine rule, two sides with the included angle or three sides mean cosine rule — then multi-step problems and bearings contexts chaining rules. Foundation stops at right-angled methods. (G20, G22, G23)

groups.title: Measures, scale drawings and bearings
groups.lead: Reading and making accurate drawings, the units mensuration answers carry, and directions given as three-figure bearings.

groups.title: Perimeter and area
groups.lead: The distance round a shape and the space inside it, from counting squares to the formulas for triangles, parallelograms and trapezia.

groups.title: Circles, arcs and sectors
groups.lead: The two circle formulas and which of them a question is really asking for, then the fractions of a circle an angle cuts.

groups.title: Prisms and cylinders
groups.lead: Volume as repeated cross-sections and surface area as an unfolded net, for cuboids, prisms and cylinders.

groups.title: Pyramids, cones and spheres
groups.lead: The pointed and curved solids: a third for anything pointed, the sphere formulas, and solids assembled from — or cut out of — simpler ones.

groups.title: Pythagoras’ theorem
groups.lead: The relation between the three sides of a right-angled triangle, run forwards, backwards, across a grid and into three dimensions.

groups.title: Right-angled trigonometry
groups.lead: The three ratios that link an angle of a right-angled triangle to its sides, used to find sides, angles and exact values.

groups.title: The sine and cosine rules
groups.lead: Higher tier: the rules that solve any triangle, right angle or not, and the area formula that needs no height.

topics.title: Vectors
topics.cardDescription: Column vectors and translations, addition, subtraction and scalar multiples, magnitude, and vector proofs.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE vectors: column notation, addition, subtraction and scalar multiples, magnitude, and vector proofs of parallel lines and collinear points.

subtopics.title: Column vectors
subtopics.description: A displacement written as a column vector, identical wherever it starts, unlike the position a coordinate names.
subtopics.coverNote: GCSE vectors are 2D column vectors only — no 3D and no i-j component notation, both A level. Cover the column as a displacement, top entry across and bottom entry up with signs, bold-letter and arrow-over-AB notation, and the contrast with the position a coordinate pair names. Both tiers. (G25)

subtopics.title: Translations as vectors
subtopics.description: Describing a translation with a column vector, the top number across and the bottom number up, signs included.
subtopics.coverNote: Describe translations by 2D column vectors, as G24 demands, and perform the translation a given vector defines, negative components included, reading the vector off corresponding vertices of object and image. The transformations context lives on Properties' Translation page; this page owns the vector viewpoint. Both tiers. (G24)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting vectors
subtopics.description: Adding component by component, or chaining arrows nose to tail for the resultant, with subtraction as adding the reverse.
subtopics.coverNote: Add and subtract column vectors component-wise and diagrammatically nose to tail, the resultant of a two-leg journey, subtraction as adding the reverse vector, parallelogram picture included. G25 keeps both diagrammatic and column forms at both tiers. Routes expressed in a and b come later in this topic. (G25)

subtopics.title: Scalar multiples of a vector
subtopics.description: Multiplying a vector by a number scales its length, and a negative scalar reverses its direction too.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiply column and letter vectors by scalars, fractions and negatives included: the length scales while the direction holds or reverses, and expressions like 2a minus 3b are evaluated componentwise. The geometric consequence — scalar multiple means parallel — is developed on the Higher Parallel vectors page. Both tiers. (G25)

subtopics.title: The magnitude of a vector
subtopics.description: The length of a vector by Pythagoras on its two components, written between modulus bars.
subtopics.coverNote: Magnitude by Pythagoras on the two components, modulus-bar notation, triples like 3-4-5 giving exact answers. Flag for the owner: no DfE clause asks for magnitude — G24 and G25 cover representation and arithmetic only — so treat this as enrichment and check the target exam board before examining it. (G25, G20)

subtopics.title: Routes around a figure
subtopics.description: Writing the path between labelled points in terms of a and b, a vector travelled backwards picking up a minus.
subtopics.coverNote: Express routes between labelled points of triangles, parallelograms and grids in terms of a and b, a vector travelled backwards picking up a minus sign, choosing paths through known vertices. Diagrammatic representation and addition keep this at both tiers under G25; midpoints, ratios and formal proofs are Higher siblings. (G25)

subtopics.title: Fractions of a vector
subtopics.description: The vector to a midpoint or ratio point on a segment, built as a fraction of the whole vector.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher on this course, as scaffolding for the braced G25 proof work: the vector to a midpoint or to a point dividing a segment in a given ratio, built as a fraction of the whole vector inside route expressions such as a plus two thirds of b minus a. (G25)

subtopics.title: Parallel vectors
subtopics.description: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, shown by factorising the expression.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, under G25's braced geometric arguments: two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other; factorise expressions like 2a plus 4b to exhibit the multiple, and state the parallel conclusion in words. Collinearity builds on this on the next page. (G25)

subtopics.title: Collinear points
subtopics.description: Proving three points lie on one straight line by showing two vectors parallel and sharing a point.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only (braced G25): prove three points collinear by showing two vectors such as AB and AC are scalar multiples, hence parallel, and share the point A — the shared-point statement being a required line of the proof, not decoration. Full multi-step arguments are the capstone sibling page. (G25)

subtopics.title: Vector proofs
subtopics.description: Setting out a complete vector argument, from routes in a and b to the parallel or collinear conclusion.

drills.skill: The vector to a midpoint or ratio point on a segment, built as a fraction of the whole vector.
drills.scope: Higher on this course, as scaffolding for the braced G25 proof work: the vector to a midpoint or to a point dividing a segment in a given ratio, built as a fraction of the whole vector inside route expressions such as a plus two thirds of b minus a. (G25)
sections: Fluency — direct questions on fractions of a vector, limited to this lesson's stated scope (4 questions).
Application — use the same skill in unfamiliar or contextual questions without introducing a later method (4 questions).
Check — questions built around the exclusions and likely misconceptions named in the lesson brief (4 questions).

drills.title: Parallel vectors
drills.description: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, shown by factorising the expression.
drills.skill: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, shown by factorising the expression.
drills.scope: Higher only, under G25's braced geometric arguments: two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other; factorise expressions like 2a plus 4b to exhibit the multiple, and state the parallel conclusion in words. Collinearity builds on this on the next page. (G25)
sections: Fluency — direct questions on parallel vectors, limited to this lesson's stated scope (4 questions).
Application — use the same skill in unfamiliar or contextual questions without introducing a later method (4 questions).
Check — questions built around the exclusions and likely misconceptions named in the lesson brief (4 questions).

drills.title: Collinear points
drills.description: Proving three points lie on one straight line by showing two vectors parallel and sharing a point.
drills.skill: Proving three points lie on one straight line by showing two vectors parallel and sharing a point.
drills.scope: Higher only (braced G25): prove three points collinear by showing two vectors such as AB and AC are scalar multiples, hence parallel, and share the point A — the shared-point statement being a required line of the proof, not decoration. Full multi-step arguments are the capstone sibling page. (G25)
sections: Fluency — direct questions on collinear points, limited to this lesson's stated scope (4 questions).
Application — use the same skill in unfamiliar or contextual questions without introducing a later method (4 questions).
Check — questions built around the exclusions and likely misconceptions named in the lesson brief (4 questions).

drills.title: Angle rules review
drills.description: Parallel lines and polygons, stating the reason each time.
drills.skill: Finding angles with the point, line, parallel-line and polygon rules, and naming the reason for every step.
sections: Fluency — angles at a point, on a straight line, vertically opposite and in a triangle, all whole degrees with a typed answer (4 questions).
Parallel lines and polygons — alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles, then interior and exterior angles of regular polygons, each paired with a single-choice reason (4 questions).
Catch — co-interior angles offered as equal, an isosceles triangle with two possible base angles, and an exterior angle taken from 180° instead of summing the opposite interiors (4 questions).

drills.title: The special quadrilaterals review
drills.description: Naming quadrilaterals from their properties, diagonals and symmetries.
drills.skill: Identifying the special quadrilaterals from side, angle, diagonal and symmetry facts.
sections: Fluency — single-choice naming of the quadrilateral fixed by stated side and angle facts, all six special quadrilaterals appearing (4 questions).
Diagonals and symmetry — typed counts of mirror lines and orders of rotational symmetry, and single-choice questions naming the shape from its diagonal properties (4 questions).
Hierarchy — true-or-false single choices such as whether every square is a rhombus, where the inclusive definitions catch shape-as-picture thinking (4 questions).

drills.title: Congruent triangles review
drills.description: Deciding whether two triangles are congruent and naming the criterion.
drills.skill: Deciding congruence from marked facts and naming the criterion that proves it.
sections: Fluency — single-choice questions naming the criterion, SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS, that the marked facts of a triangle pair satisfy (4 questions).
Application — congruent-or-not-provable decisions with the facts given in words, including pairs that need the shared side spotted (4 questions).
Catch — two sides with a non-included angle, and three matched angles, offered beside genuine criteria; both must be rejected (4 questions).

drills.title: Similar shapes review
drills.description: Scale factors and missing lengths in similar triangles and shapes.
drills.skill: Finding scale factors and missing lengths in similar shapes, corresponding sides paired correctly.
sections: Fluency — integer and half-integer scale factors from a matched pair of sides, then a missing length by multiplying, every answer exact (4 questions).
Application — nested and bow-tie triangle configurations where the corresponding sides must be identified before scaling, whole-number answers throughout (4 questions).
Catch — problems where adding the difference between sides gives a plausible wrong answer, and a shared-angle pair that is not similar at all (4 questions).

drills.title: Transformations review
drills.description: Performing and describing reflections, rotations, translations and enlargements on axes.
drills.skill: Applying the four transformations on coordinate axes and describing them fully.
sections: Fluency — image coordinates of a marked vertex after a stated reflection, rotation about the origin or column-vector translation, typed as integers (4 questions).
Describing — single-choice complete descriptions of the transformation mapping object to image, distractors omitting the centre, direction or mirror line (4 questions).
Catch — reflections in y = x set against the axes, rotations with the direction reversed, and an enlargement whose scale factor is read from the wrong side pair (4 questions).

drills.title: Circle theorems review
drills.description: Applying each theorem and justifying the reason.
drills.skill: Finding angles with the circle theorems and naming the theorem that justifies each step.
sections: Fluency — one theorem per figure: centre and circumference, semicircle, same segment and cyclic quadrilateral, every angle a whole number of degrees (4 questions).
Application — figures chaining two or three theorems, tangents and the alternate segment included, with the intermediate angle asked first (4 questions).
Justification — single-choice questions picking the theorem that earns the reason mark, the tempting wrong theorem sharing the same diagram (4 questions).

drills.title: Solids, nets and plans review
drills.description: Counting faces, edges and vertices, matching nets, and reading plans and elevations.
drills.skill: Recognising solids from their counts, nets, plans and elevations.
sections: Fluency — typed counts of the faces, edges and vertices of named solids, prisms and pyramids on stated bases included (4 questions).
Nets and views — single-choice matching of a net to its solid and of a plan or elevation to the drawn solid (4 questions).
Catch — arrangements of six squares that do not fold into a cube, and lookalike elevations taken from the wrong direction (4 questions).

drills.title: Bearings and scale review
drills.description: Three-figure bearings, back bearings and scale conversions, all in whole degrees.
drills.skill: Reading, writing and calculating three-figure bearings, and converting scaled lengths.
sections: Fluency — writing directions as three-figure bearings with leading zeros required, and reading the bearing of B from A off a marked diagram (4 questions).
Back bearings and journeys — the return bearing by adding or subtracting 180°, and two-leg journeys using angle facts at the turn, whole degrees throughout (4 questions).
Scale — converting between map and ground with ratio scales like 1:25 000 and drawing scales like 1 cm to 5 km, the unit change being the catch (4 questions).

drills.title: Perimeter and area review
drills.description: Triangles, parallelograms, trapezia and composite shapes, with lengths recovered from areas.
drills.skill: Finding perimeters and areas of straight-sided shapes, and running the formulas backwards.
sections: Fluency — areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms and trapezia from labelled integer sides and heights (4 questions).
Composite — L-shapes and joined shapes needing missing sides deduced first, with area and perimeter asked in separate questions (4 questions).
Catch — figures labelled with both slant and perpendicular heights, and a missing base recovered from a stated area (4 questions).

drills.title: Area, surface area and volume review
drills.description: Circles, sectors, prisms, cones, spheres and frustums, exact in terms of π.
drills.skill: Calculating circle measures and solid volumes exactly, answers left in terms of π.
sections: Fluency — circumference and area from an integer radius or diameter, answered as the coefficient of π (4 questions).
Arcs and sectors — arc lengths and sector areas for angles like 60°, 90° and 120° that leave exact fractions, plus one reversed to find the angle (4 questions).
Solids — volumes of cylinders, cones, pyramids and spheres with dimensions chosen so the thirds cancel, ending with a frustum by subtracting the missing cone (4 questions).

drills.title: Pythagoras’ theorem review
drills.description: Hypotenuses, shorter sides and cuboid diagonals, built on Pythagorean triples.
drills.skill: Applying Pythagoras’ theorem forwards, backwards and in three dimensions, with triple-based exact answers.
sections: Fluency — hypotenuses and shorter sides from Pythagorean triples like 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17, scaled copies included (4 questions).
Application — distances between coordinate points and diagonals of rectangles, each engineered to land on a triple (4 questions).
Catch — a converse decision from three given sides, adding when the hypotenuse is known, and a cuboid diagonal such as 3 by 4 by 12 giving exactly 13 (4 questions).

drills.title: Trigonometry review
drills.description: Right-angled triangles and the exact values, no calculator needed.
drills.skill: Choosing and using the right trigonometric ratio in right-angled triangles, with exact values throughout.
sections: Fluency — labelling opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, then sides found with tan 45° = 1, sin 30° = ½ and cos 60° = ½ (4 questions).
Exact values — recalling sin, cos and tan at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and angles recovered from exact ratios like tan θ = √3 (4 questions).
Catch — a division where multiplication is expected, opposite and adjacent swapped by a rotated triangle, and an elevation angle placed at the wrong vertex (4 questions).

drills.title: The sine and cosine rules review
drills.description: Sides, angles and areas in non-right-angled triangles, engineered to come out exactly.
drills.skill: Solving non-right-angled triangles with the sine rule, cosine rule and ½ab sin C.
sections: Fluency — sine rule sides and angles with pairings like 30° opposite 5 and 90° opposite 10, every ratio exact (4 questions).
Cosine rule — third sides with included angles of 60° or 120°, such as sides 3 and 5 around 120° giving exactly 7, and one angle recovered from three sides (4 questions).
Areas and choice — ½ab sin C with 30° angles for integer areas, and single-choice decisions naming which rule the given facts allow (4 questions).

drills.title: Vector arithmetic review
drills.description: Column vector addition, subtraction, scalar multiples and magnitude.
drills.skill: Calculating with column vectors: sums, differences, scalar multiples and magnitudes.
sections: Fluency — adding and subtracting column vectors and multiplying by scalars, negative components throughout (4 questions).
Application — the vector translating one given point to another, resultants of two-leg journeys, and a missing component from a stated resultant (4 questions).
Catch — magnitudes built on 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 components, and a distractor treating a vector as the coordinates of a point (4 questions).

drills.title: Vector geometry review
drills.description: Routes in a and b, midpoints, parallel vectors and collinearity.
drills.skill: Building vector expressions around a figure and arguing parallelism and collinearity from them.
sections: Fluency — single-choice expressions in a and b for marked routes around triangles and parallelograms, reversed vectors negated (4 questions).
Fractions — vectors to midpoints and to points dividing a segment in a given ratio, chosen from simplified expressions (4 questions).
Proof steps — single-choice justifications naming why two expressions show vectors parallel or points collinear, where a common factor must be extracted first (4 questions).
